clue.text: "One good horse-shoe is worth about two and a quarter sermons" (De Quincey)

definitions.text: "One good horse-shoe is worth about two and a quarter sermons" (De Quincey)

parts.words: "One good horse-shoe is worth about two and a quarter sermons" (De Quincey)
parts.note: a quotation from De Quincey with one word left out: the kind of sermon preached at Easter from the pulpit of a London ... churchyard

explanation.surface: A wry De Quincey line ranking a horseshoe above a pile of sermons.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver supplies the word missing before 'sermons' in De Quincey's sentence; the Spital Sermons were annual Easter sermons in London, once preached at the hospital of St Mary Spital.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the annual London Easter sermons comes from an old word for a hospital, and it fills the gap in the quotation.

clue.text: Neil Simon's Spanish place sounded sweet

explanation.surface: A remark that the Spanish square in a Neil Simon play had a sweet sound.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Simon wrote the play Plaza Suite, and 'sounded sweet' plays on suite sounding like sweet; a plaza is a Spanish town square.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaza is a public square in a Spanish town, and the word also begins the title of Neil Simon's comedy Plaza Suite.

explanation.surface: Asking whether a page by Maugham shook in the reader's hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Maugham's story collection is The Trembling of a Leaf, and a page is a leaf of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Quivering is shaking with small movements, and a leaf (page) in Maugham's title does just that.

parts.note: reads like grudging agreement, but points to a market town whose fair Housman wrote about in A Shropshire Lad

explanation.surface: A grudging concession that something is acceptable to the poet Housman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair enough' sounds like an idiom of agreement; here 'fair' is a town fair. Housman's poem 'The Lent Lily' and others mention the fair of this Shropshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: A Shropshire market town whose fair appears in Housman's poems of A Shropshire Lad.

clue.text: His head of state was barely visible

definitions.text: His head of state was barely visible

parts.words: His head of state was barely visible
parts.note: the storyteller whose emperor paraded in imaginary new clothes, so his ruler was seen almost naked

explanation.surface: A remark about a leader who kept a very low public profile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely visible' means hardly seen, but here it means visible in the bare: in the Danish author's tale The Emperor's New Clothes the ruler walks out naked.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish fairy-tale writer created the emperor whose invisible robes left him naked before his subjects.

parts.note: a scarlet room or study is a whimsical gloss on the title of the first Sherlock Holmes novel

explanation.surface: Asking about a red-painted room in Conan Doyle's house.
explanation.walkthrough: Den means a study and red means scarlet, so the clue is a literal paraphrase of Conan Doyle's first Holmes story title.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's 1887 novel introducing Sherlock Holmes, whose title literally pairs a private room with a bright red colour.

clue.text: Exquisite sort of regime from Gascoigne

explanation.surface: Praising a refined diet devised by the Elizabethan poet Gascoigne.
explanation.walkthrough: George Gascoigne wrote A Delicate Diet for Daintiemouthed Droonkardes, and a diet is a regime.
explanation.definitionFit: Exquisite means fine and dainty, and Gascoigne's tract is titled A Delicate Diet.

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps
Odin is the chief god of Norse mythology

explanation.surface: Describing a sculptor posing as a river deity.
explanation.definitionFit: The French artist who made The Thinker and The Kiss was a famous sculptor.

parts.note: Rosten's comic book about a night-school pupil learning English is titled after the pupil's schooling

explanation.surface: Leo Rosten took on the job of teaching his character Hyman Kaplan.
explanation.walkthrough: Leo Rosten's 1937 book is The Education of H*Y*M*A*N K*A*P*L*A*N, about an immigrant at evening classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Schooling is the subject and title word of Rosten's book about Kaplan's English lessons.

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of the two following words appear in an odd arrangement

explanation.surface: A strange theatrical contract involving the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges ACTORS and DEAL together.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything relating to priests and their office.

clue.text: One of those heard in the night by Brecht

definitions.text: One of those heard in the night by Brecht

parts.words: One of those heard in the night by Brecht
parts.note: Brecht's early play is titled for percussion instruments beating in the dark

explanation.surface: Something heard after dark in a Brecht drama.
explanation.walkthrough: Brecht's 1922 play is Trommeln in der Nacht, Drums in the Night; the clue asks for one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A percussion instrument, one of those in the title of Brecht's play Drums in the Night.

parts.note: the phrase 'there's no ... between them' describes friends without lingering hostility

explanation.surface: A saying about the harmony shared by friends.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'there is no bad blood between us' means no ill feeling; the capital F hints at a title.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names hostility or ill feeling, which true friends are said to lack.

indicators.note: sort here is a verb, so the letters of the fabric name are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A kind of synthetic thread used in spinning.
explanation.walkthrough: Dacron is a polyester yarn, so 'yarn-spinner' looks like a textile term; it means a storyteller, the novelist Joseph Conrad.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinner of yarns tells stories, and Joseph Conrad was a celebrated novelist.

clue.text: Wine from Benedick's Padua, still sparkling

indicators.note: from shows that the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A sparkling wine Benedick might drink in Padua.
explanation.walkthrough: Benedick in Much Ado About Nothing comes from Padua; the wine sits inside 'Padua, still', and sparkling describes the Italian wine.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian sparkling white wine from Piedmont, named after its home town.

parts.note: one means single
a ton is a large weight

explanation.surface: A lone heavy sailor in a Defoe story.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's novel Captain Singleton follows a sailor and pirate.

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of I PRINTED take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A claim to have printed a Thomas Hardy novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy novel' looks like a book by Thomas Hardy; Hardy is the definition and 'novel' rearranges I PRINTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy in the sense of brave and fearless is a synonym.

indicators.note: unexpected suggests the letters of the two words turn up in a surprising order

explanation.surface: Bishops showing a surprising burst of sociability.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unexpected' rearranges SOCIAL PEP.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes church government by bishops.

clue.text: Elderly self-obsessed pedant from the time of Caesar's murder?

annotationWithheld.why: "Elderly self-obsessed pedant from the time of Caesar's murder?": the pedant is Middlemarch's Casaubon, but no parse of 'from the time of Caesar's murder' builds the name
annotationWithheld.clue: Elderly self-obsessed pedant from the time of Caesar's murder?

clue.text: Puzzles a poor horse runs into

parts.note: a nag is a worn-out horse
rams means crashes into

explanation.surface: A broken-down horse collides with something.
explanation.definitionFit: Word puzzles made by rearranging letters, the subject of crosswords like this.

clue.text: Locals where Mortimer and others have been called to the bar

definitions.text: where Mortimer and others have been called to the bar

explanation.surface: Pubs where John Mortimer and fellow lawyers got called to the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub. John Mortimer, creator of Rumpole, was a barrister called to the bar at one of London's Inns of Court.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are pubs, and the Inns of Court are the London societies that admit barristers.

parts.note: a line from Childe Harold with the goddess's name left out after 'august'

explanation.surface: A Byron line addressing an ancient, majestic figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, canto II, reads 'Ancient of days! august Athena!'; the solver supplies the missing name of the Greek goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of wisdom, patron of Athens, is the one Byron addresses in the line.

clue.text: Russian composer with connection in Georgia

indicators.note: in places the word for connection inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
a link is a connection

explanation.surface: A Russian composer with ties to Georgia.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikhail Glinka is regarded as the father of Russian classical music.

parts.note: Shaw's novel is titled for work done after dark

explanation.surface: Describing the kind of writing Irwin Shaw produced.
explanation.walkthrough: Irwin Shaw wrote the 1975 novel Nightwork; 'sort of work' asks for its first part.
explanation.definitionFit: Work done after dark, as in the title of Irwin Shaw's novel Nightwork.

explanation.surface: A new dance for goat-footed woodland creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldous Huxley's novel took its title from Marlowe's Edward II, where satyrs 'with their goat feet dance an antic hay'.
explanation.definitionFit: Huxley's 1923 novel and a grotesque country dance in Marlowe's play share the name.

parts.note: not Othello but the villain of Titus Andronicus, lover of the Goth queen Tamora

explanation.surface: The Moor in Shakespeare adored by a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shakespeare's Moor' suggests Othello, but he is too long; the Moor loved by Tamora, Queen of the Goths, is the villain of Titus Andronicus.
explanation.definitionFit: The scheming Moor of Titus Andronicus is the lover of Tamora, Queen of the Goths.

annotationWithheld.why: "Landseer subject by Laurel?": Landseer's stag fits, but no reading of 'by Laurel' as held gives the word

clue.text: Achiever said to have produced this ball recreation area

definitions.text: Achiever said to have produced this

parts.note: a bullet was once a ball of shot
a park is a public space for recreation

explanation.surface: An achiever reportedly made a ball playground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Achiever said' sounds like Cheever: John Cheever wrote the 1969 novel Bullet Park.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cheever, whose name sounds like achiever, wrote the suburban novel Bullet Park.

clue.text: That of Joe Eszterhas was basic

definitions.text: That of Joe Eszterhas was basic

parts.words: That of Joe Eszterhas was basic
parts.note: Eszterhas wrote the thriller film whose title pairs basic with an inborn drive

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict that the screenwriter's work was simple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basic' seems to mean crude; Joe Eszterhas wrote the screenplay of the 1992 film Basic Instinct.
explanation.definitionFit: An inborn drive or urge, the second word of the film title Basic Instinct.

annotationWithheld.why: "Current country of woodstock cavalier": AD (current era) + LAND fits, but 'woodstock cavalier' does not define the entry as held
